newsitem.title: INDIA: BANK OF NOVA SCOTIA SEEKS INDIAN GOLD LICENCE.
newsitem.headline: BANK OF NOVA SCOTIA SEEKS INDIAN GOLD LICENCE.

text.p: Canada's Bank of Nova Scotia has sought a licence to import gold into India following the government's decision to liberalise gold trade, a senior official of the bank said on Monday.
"We have submitted an application for a gold licence," Douglas H. Stewart, the bank's senior vice-president for South Asia, told Reuters in an interview.
Earlier this month, addressing a seminar on gold in New Delhi, a top official of the country's central bank said more banks would be allowed to import gold into India.

At present, the government-run State Bank of India (SBI) and state-run trading company MMTC Ltd are allowed to import gold for supplying to jewellers. The government wants to broaden the list because gold imports are expected to rise following a drive to boost the country's jewellery exports.
According to Bombay Bullion Association president Makhan Lal Damani, India's gold imports in calendar 1997 are expected to touch 500 tonnes against 409 tonnes in the previous year.
He said the new policy measures might take some time to materialise, and when they did they would boost gold imports and jewellery exports.
India, the world's largest consumer of gold, has in the last few years liberalised its gold imports as part of its radical reforms and to curb smuggling of the metal into the country.
Expatriate Indians are currently allowed to import up to 10 kg of gold once every six months, subject to a duty of 220 rupees per 10 grammes.
Gold can also be imported against special import licences by those earning foreign exchange. These licences can be bought by any user, at a market-driven premium.
"We have a lot of expertise in handling gold at the precious metals division of Scotia Capital Markets," Stewart said.
"We would take the responsibility in putting resources in India (after getting a licence)," he said. The bank now has three branches in India -- in New Delhi, Bombay and Coimbatore.
Indian jewellers, unhedged at present, feel that banks, especially foreign ones, have the know-how to deal with gold imports and supplies.

V.M Kapoor, president of the Bombay-based Gold Jewellery Exporters' Association, said he would expect more banks to handle gold imports in the near future. "These banks can set up gold accounts," he said. India's gold stocks, existing mostly in the form of household jewellery and ornaments, are estimated at around 9,000 tonnes.
Stewart said the bank could import and store gold and offer gold loans. "Everything depends on the terms of the licence."
Bankers and analysts are awaiting detailed guidelines from the government on gold imports.
There has been speculation in the inter-bank market that by allowing banks to act as intermediaries, the government wants to promote gold-dollar swap deals.
This would reduce the pressure on RBI, which has been buying dollars in recent months to arrest the rupee's rise on the back of large capital inflows, dealers said.
